description: Somos Earth Explorers 67, un grupo de estudiantes interesados en tecnología, programación y el cuidado del planeta. Participaremos en el NASA Space Apps Challenge para aprender y crear soluciones sobre la Tierra y sus cambios. Tenemos habilidades en programación, diseño, investigación y trabajo en equipo, y buscamos personas responsables, creativas y con ganas de aportar.
summary:
EARTH//TRACE is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) web platform that turns NASA Earth observation data into discoveries anyone can understand. It answers the challenge’s core questions: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is significant.

Users become “planet detectives.” The Earth Explorer maps 110 countries across 8 regions by phenomenon: ice, drought, wildfires, floods, coasts, water and forests. Each country profile links its official national agency with the NASA datasets that measure it, such as GRACE/GRACE-FO, Landsat, MODIS and GPM IMERG. The Data Lab applies the Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope to tell real change from noise. Using real NASA JPL data, it shows Greenland losing about 268 gigatonnes of ice per year (p < 0.001). Three real detective cases (Lake Enriquillo, the Aral Sea and Greenland), missions, badges and a passport make learning feel like a game. An AI assistant on every page answers questions without inventing numbers. The assistant also works on any website through a browser extension or a one-line plugin. Developers can reuse the country data through a free public JSON API.

This matters because NASA data is public but scattered and technical. EARTH//TRACE puts it in the hands of students, journalists and decision-makers, on computer and phone.
details:
What it does and how it works

EARTH//TRACE is a gamified web platform that helps anyone detect what is changing on Earth, where, how much, and whether the change is significant. It works in any browser, on computer or phone, with no installation or account.

  • Earth Explorer: an interactive map of 110 countries in 8 regions, colored by their main phenomenon: ice, drought, wildfires, floods, coasts, water or forests. Each country profile shows what is changing and a research question. It also names the official national agency that measures the change on the ground and the NASA datasets that measure it from space, with a direct link to NASA Worldview.
  • Discovery Center: each phenomenon explained with everyday analogies, linked to the countries where it happens.
  • EARTH//TRACE Game: detective cases built on real data: Lake Enriquillo (Dominican Republic), the Aral Sea and Greenland. Players first guess whether a change is real or just noise, then check the evidence.
  • Data Lab: applies the Mann-Kendall trend test and Sen’s slope to any time series, including CSV files downloaded from NASA Giovanni or AppEEARS. With real NASA JPL GRACE/GRACE-FO data, it shows Greenland losing about 268 gigatonnes of ice per year (p < 0.001).
  • Global Cases and Workspace: findings become exportable case files; users earn XP, ranks, badges and a country “passport.”
  • AI assistant: a floating planet on every page opens a chat. The chat combines AI with the platform’s data, cites official sources, names the satellite that measures each phenomenon, and is instructed never to invent numbers. If the AI is unavailable, it still answers from platform data.
  • Beyond the platform: a Chrome/Edge extension puts the assistant on any website. A one-line plugin lets schools and media embed it. A free public JSON API and an AI Skill let developers reuse the data.

Benefits and expected impact

NASA data is public but scattered, technical and hard to interpret. EARTH//TRACE makes it understandable for students, teachers, journalists and local decision-makers. It also teaches how scientists tell real change from noise. We started from the Dominican Republic and scaled to 110 countries, so any community can investigate its own environment. We expect it to support climate education in classrooms, more accurate environmental reporting and citizen science.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Python
  • Libraries: D3.js and TopoJSON for maps and charts; NumPy, SciPy, xarray and earthaccess for data processing
  • NASA data: GRACE/GRACE-FO (JPL Mascons), Landsat/HLS, MODIS, GPM IMERG, SWOT, NASA Worldview, Giovanni, AppEEARS and Earthdata
  • Infrastructure: GitHub Pages for hosting; Cloudflare Workers as a secure server for the AI, so the API key is never exposed; Google Gemini API as the assistant’s model; Chrome extension (Manifest V3)
  • Development assistance: Claude (Anthropic) helped with coding and writing. The team designed, reviewed and tested all content.
  • Hardware: personal laptops and smartphones for development and testing

Creativity

Instead of a typical data dashboard, EARTH//TRACE turns science into a detective story: the planet “leaves evidence” and users learn to read it. The game asks players to predict before revealing results, which builds scientific thinking. The assistant is not trapped inside one website: it follows the user to any page they are reading.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: real NASA data, statistical significance, official sources, and an AI that does not invent figures
  • Accessibility: a highly legible typeface, high contrast, keyboard navigation and a reduced-motion option
  • Language: full English and Spanish versions
  • Mobile-first design: an app-like experience on phones, for users without a computer
  • Privacy and security: no accounts, progress stored only in the user’s browser, and API keys kept on a secure server
  • Reliability: the platform keeps working even when the AI is unavailable
  • Cost: free to use and free to host
